description: I am Waseka Mehrin,a first year student of BUET. I'm into tech projects.
summary: SHELTER is health monitoring software that astronauts run themselves. On a Mars mission a message to Earth can take up to 22 minutes each way, so crews must spot changes in their own health. Each day the astronaut does a two-minute check-in (sleep, mood, stress, exercise, symptoms, cabin CO2), a 3-minute reaction-time test (PVT-B) in the browser and a 15-second pulse count, and can add heart-beat data from any wearable. SHELTER turns this into one clear answer: what needs action today, why, and the published source behind each rule. It covers the challenge's four stressors (space radiation, isolation and confinement, altered gravity, closed cabin air) and four health systems (immune, bone, heart, behavior), comparing each indicator with NASA limits or with the astronaut's own normal range. Radiation comes from NASA OMNI2 and NOAA GOES solar-storm data: SHELTER computes the dose in the suit, cabin and storm shelter and tracks each astronaut's dose budget. The astronaut's state also adapts the storm rules; for example, no spacewalk starts after a failed alertness test. Decisions are tested by replaying storms hour by hour without hindsight. The log is saved only on the astronaut's device.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

On long missions astronauts carry much of the responsibility for spotting changes in their own health. SHELTER makes that a five-minute daily routine with one clear result. The home screen answers "what needs action today?", lists each action with the measured value, what to do and the published source, and shows four health systems (immune, bone, heart and circulation, behavior and cognition) and the four mission stressors from the challenge.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Gather (by the astronaut, no extra hardware): a daily check-in (sleep, wake time, mood, stress, resistive exercise, cabin CO2 reading, symptoms); a 3-minute Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT-B) that runs in any browser; a 15-second pulse count by tapping; optional heart-beat (RR) intervals from any wearable for heart-rate variability.

2. Evaluate: each indicator is compared with a published limit or with the astronaut's own normal range, learned from their first 5 check-ins.

- Radiation: cosmic-ray dose plus solar-storm doses, against NCRP-132 30-day and annual limits and the NASA-STD-3001 career limit; any single exposure above the 0.7 Gy acute-radiation-syndrome threshold is flagged.

- Alertness: PVT-B lapses (reaction time of 355 ms or more, Basner et al. 2011) against the astronaut's baseline.

- Sleep: the two-process model of sleep (Process S), where 1.0 means rested.

- Heart: resting heart rate and HRV (RMSSD, SDNN, after artefact removal) against the baseline.

- Cabin air: 7-day CO2 average against NASA's 2.5 mmHg headache guidance and the 3 mmHg NASA-STD-3001 limit; headache odds double per +1 mmHg (Law et al. 2014).

- Bone: adherence to the prescribed resistive exercise, with the 1.1-1.6 % per month bone loss at stake (LeBlanc et al. 2000).

- Immune: fever, infection, rash and cold-sore symptoms (Crucian et al.).

3. Act: OK / Watch / Act now, each with the reason and source.

4. Adapt: the astronaut's state changes SHELTER's solar-storm rules. A shrinking dose budget means sheltering earlier; a failed alertness test or high sleep pressure means no spacewalk starts until a re-test.

THE RADIATION ENGINE (NASA DATA)

SHELTER reads hourly proton fluxes above 1 to 60 MeV from NASA SPDF OMNI2 for historical storms and live GOES protons from NOAA SWPC. It removes the quiet-time background using only past data, builds an energy spectrum, and slows each proton through the suit (0.3 g/cm2), cabin (~10) and storm shelter (~31) using the Bethe formula, which matches NIST PSTAR within 1.3 %. It then computes dose to skin, eye and blood-forming organs (ICRP-60 quality factor). NASA DONKI flares, CMEs and SEP onsets mark the timeline. The dose engine is compared with radiation measured inside the Mars Science Laboratory on its way to Mars (MSL/RAD, Guo et al. 2015). Any replayed storm's dose can be added to an astronaut's health log.

WHY IT CAN BE TRUSTED

- No hindsight: every result for a day uses only data up to that day; unit tests change all later data and check nothing earlier moves.

- Missing data never reads as "safe": during a data gap SHELTER holds its state.

- The OMNI2 reader is tested on real NASA OMNI2 lines.

- 101 automated tests, 94 % line coverage.

- Every threshold that is a team choice is labelled as one in the app. SHELTER is decision support for the crew and flight surgeon, not a diagnosis.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Astronauts get one daily answer and keep their data on their own device. Flight surgeons get trends with sources despite the communication delay. Mission planners get storm rules matched to each crew member. Students and the public can take the reaction test and replay real solar storms in a browser.

CREATIVITY

SHELTER links space-weather physics to personal health monitoring: the same engine that computes a solar storm's dose behind the shelter walls also updates the astronaut's dose budget, and the astronaut's alertness and dose budget feed back into the storm and spacewalk rules.

TOOLS

Python 3.12 and NumPy (physics, data, health models), a standard-library web server and WSGI API, HTML5 Canvas charts with no external libraries, deployed on Vercel. Works on phones, tablets and laptops; run locally, the health monitor works with no internet at all.

FACTORS CONSIDERED AND LIMITS

Privacy: the log is saved only in the browser, and the server keeps nothing. Honesty: the demo astronaut is synthetic and labelled. Not covered: blood counts, bone scans, blood pressure, circadian phase (Process C), secondary neutrons in the radiation transport; GOES measures at Earth, not at a spacecraft far away. The 60-second reaction test is a demo; the validated test is the 3-minute PVT-B.

AI USE

Parts of the code, tests, documentation and presentation were drafted with an AI assistant (Claude, Anthropic) and reviewed by the team.
